what_it_does: Every program running on a modern processor works with virtual memory addresses — convenient labels that the hardware quietly translates to real physical locations on the chip's memory chips. A small, fast lookup table called a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) remembers recent translations so the processor does not have to recompute them constantly; when a needed translation is not there (a 'TLB miss'), the processor stalls and looks it up the slow way. Large server applications often have sprawling instruction code (the executable program itself) that does not fit in the TLB, causing frequent stalls specifically for instruction fetches — which is particularly damaging because stalling on an instruction means the whole pipeline freezes rather than just delaying one data item. This paper argues that the TLB and the nearby instruction cache (a small fast copy of recently used code) should coordinate their eviction decisions instead of operating independently. When one structure is about to throw out a memory page, it tells the other, preventing the wasteful situation where one structure evicts something the other just refetched. The policy also gives priority to instruction accesses based on how often and how recently each code page has been used.
